summary: This RFC reproduces the National Research Council report that compared the DoD Internet Protocol and TCP with the ISO Internet Protocol and Transport Protocol class 4 (TP-4).

eli5.summary: A group of experts studied two sets of network rules and wrote a report on which is better. This copies the report.

questions: what was the nrc report on transport protocols
should the dod use tcp or tp4
subtitle: A government study comparing two transport protocols for military networks.

tldr.problem: The DoD and NBS disagreed on which transport protocol should be the standard: the DoD's TCP or the ISO's new TP-4. Both agencies needed a recommendation to resolve the conflict.
tldr.mechanism: A National Research Council committee studied both protocols side by side, examining their functional equivalence, implementation status, security properties, costs, and transition implications for DoD networks.
tldr.outcome: The committee recommended that the DoD adopt TP-4 as a costandard alongside TCP, with options for either immediate adoption or a phased approach after demonstration. This reflected a strategic shift toward international standards while acknowledging DoD's existing TCP infrastructure.

facts.label: Study authorized by
facts.value: Department of Defense and National Bureau of Standards

today: RFC 942's recommendation to adopt TP-4 as a costandard reflected the beginning of a long transition in the DoD toward ISO standards, though TCP/IP ultimately became the dominant protocol suite worldwide. The report illustrates the tension between military-specific requirements and international standardization, a challenge that persists in network protocol development.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.content:
RFC 942 is not a protocol specification; it is a government report. The National Research Council, an advisory body established by the Academy of Sciences, was asked in 1983 by the DoD and NBS to resolve a standards conflict. The Department of Defense had standardized on TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and IP (Internet Protocol) after years of development in the ARPANET research program. The National Bureau of Standards, working with the ISO, was promoting a new international standard: TP-4 (ISO Transport Protocol class 4) and an ISO Internet Protocol.

Both protocols were designed to handle reliable, ordered delivery of data streams. The question was not whether both could work, but which one the DoD should commit to and how to manage a transition if any.
sections.eli5: Two government agencies picked different rule books for sending messages reliably over networks. A group of experts was asked to study both and tell the military which to use.

sections.title: DoD Operational Needs and Requirements
sections.content:
The DoD has unique requirements that shape protocol choices. These include survivability (networks must function even after nodes and links are destroyed), security (traffic and data must be protected through encryption and access control), precedence (priority-based quality of service), robustness (the system must handle unexpected situations), availability (elements must be continuously available), and interoperability (different parts of DoD must be able to communicate).

These operational needs translate into five technical requirements: functional specifications that meet operational needs, maximum interoperability, minimum procurement and development costs, ease of transition to new protocols, and manageability. The committee evaluated both TCP and TP-4 against these criteria.
sections.eli5: The military has special needs: its networks must keep working even when parts break, messages must be kept secret, important messages go first, and different military branches must be able to talk to each other. The rule book has to handle all of this.

sections.title: Technical Comparison of TCP and TP-4
sections.content:
The committee found that TCP and TP-4 are functionally equivalent and provide essentially similar services. Both offer reliable, in-order delivery of data. Although they differ in specific areas—such as data transfer interface, flow control, connection establishment, and out-of-band services—neither protocol is intrinsically superior. The services are provided in different ways, but the differences do not compromise DoD requirements. Existing applications may need modification to move from TCP to TP-4, but new applications can be written for either protocol with similar effort.

Security-related properties are sufficiently equivalent that no significant technical point favors one over the other. TCP has an advantage in maturity—it has been implemented since the mid-1970s and was in widespread use—while TP-4 had not yet been implemented in large operational systems, though it had received endorsement from many commercial vendors worldwide and was demonstrated at industry conferences.
sections.eli5: Both rule books do basically the same job—they both get messages there safely and in the right order. TCP is older and more proven. TP-4 is newer and will probably be used more by other countries and companies.

sections.title: Economic and Strategic Considerations
sections.content:
A major factor in the decision is commercial availability. TCP implementations were already commercial products available from multiple vendors, but the DoD controlled the specification and bore development costs. TP-4, being an ISO standard, would benefit from widespread commercial development, spreading costs across the vendor base and allowing the DoD to use off-the-shelf products.

The RFC notes that by using commercial products, the DoD could save 30 to 80 percent on development, production, and maintenance costs. Additionally, by committing early to TP-4 as a standard, the DoD would benefit from the worldwide market demand and vendor competition driving TP-4 improvements.

However, the DoD had massive investments in TCP infrastructure. Networks like MILNET, MINET, SACDIN, and DODIIS were expanding, and converting all of them would be expensive if not managed carefully. The committee had to balance the long-term advantages of ISO standardization with the short-term costs of transition.
sections.eli5: TP-4 is more popular around the world, so companies will make cheaper products for it. But the military has already spent a lot of money on TCP networks, so switching everything at once would be very expensive.

sections.title: Committee Recommendations and Options
sections.content:
The committee presented three options. Option 1 (the majority recommendation) was for the DoD to immediately adopt TP-4 as a costandard with TCP. New networks and major upgrades would specify TP-4, while existing TCP networks could continue operating. Contracts for new systems would be awarded only to contractors offering commercial TP-4 products. The DoD would develop military specifications for TP-4 and establish validation test facilities.

Option 2 (minority recommendation) deferred commitment until a successful demonstration of TP-4 in military networks, lasting at most 18 months. This reduced risk but delayed the financial benefits of early standardization.

Option 3 was to defer any decision indefinitely and continue with TCP. This minimized short-term risk and cost but meant missing opportunities for commercial product availability and international interoperability.

The committee believed all three options equally satisfied functional DoD objectives, but Option 1 provided the most rapid path to commercial products and external interoperability. The DoD would eventually face pressure to standardize on TP-4 as the international standard.
sections.eli5: The experts said: Option 1 is to switch to TP-4 now for new networks and save money long-term. Option 2 is to try TP-4 first in a test, then decide. Option 3 is to keep using TCP and forget about switching. Each choice has trade-offs.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content: The RFC concludes that both TCP and TP-4 are technically sound and could meet DoD requirements. The choice is not about technical superiority but about timing, cost, and strategic positioning. By adopting TP-4 as a costandard, the DoD could align with international standards, benefit from commercial development, and improve interoperability with NATO, intelligence agencies, and other parts of the federal government. However, the transition must be managed carefully to avoid disrupting operational networks.
sections.eli5: Both rule books work fine. The decision is about money and strategy: switching earlier means saving money later by using cheaper commercial products, but it costs more to make the switch.
